title: The engineered stone prohibition and what it means on a job
audience: Stone and terrazzo restoration technicians, leading hands, estimators and the person who takes job enquiries
learningOutcomes: State when the national engineered stone prohibition started and when the import ban started
Explain why installed engineered stone does not have to be removed and why work on it is still restricted
Identify the points on which the sources differ and explain how this course handles them
Decline or refer an engineered stone job in a way that does not suggest the work is lawful
referencesAtStart: Official sources for this lesson: DEWR, Prohibition on the use of engineered stone (no date shown); ASEA, Engineered stone prohibition (no date shown); SA, Engineered stone ban (title dated 1 July 2024; no publication date shown); SWA, When does a PCBU need to notify the WHS regulator of plans to process legacy engineered stone (August 2025, as shown on the document); WorkSafe Victoria, Working with engineered stone (reviewed 27/08/2024); Customs (Prohibited Imports) Amendment (Engineered Stone) Regulations 2024 (F2024L01600), explanatory material (registered 6 Dec 2024; import ban commences 1 Jan 2025).

instruction.heading: What is banned and from when
instruction.body: The national prohibition on engineered stone benchtops, panels and slabs commenced on 1 July 2024. The DEWR page dates the import ban to 1 January 2025. Processing and installation are covered: the Asbestos Safety and SA Government pages both say so, and the explanatory material to the import instrument describes the domestic ban in the same terms, with 'processing' defined in WHS Regulation 529A. The DEWR page does not address processing or installation. The explanatory material also notes that some jurisdictions delayed full implementation to 31 December 2024. Porcelain and sintered stone are excluded, and so are finished items that need no processing. The instrument's explanatory material lists further products outside engineered stone, including concrete and cement products, bricks, ceramic tiles, grout, mortar and plasterboard. The WHS Regulation 529A text itself was not read this session, so its exact wording is partly checked.

instruction.heading: What installed stone means for you
instruction.body: Installed engineered stone does not have to be removed. The SA Government page adds that installed stone can be used safely while it stays undisturbed. The practical point is that the work is the problem, not the stone sitting in the kitchen. Removing, repairing, modifying or disposing of installed engineered stone is restricted. Asbestos Safety says that controlled processing of legacy stone for repair, removal, minor modification or disposal may be allowed, and that the WHS regulator must be notified before the work. Safe Work Australia's guidance of August 2025 says notification is required when work involves processing engineered stone, that the regulator does not need to approve the work before it starts, and that the notice should be kept for five years. WorkSafe Victoria says the uncontrolled dry cutting of legacy engineered stone is not permitted in Victoria, and that a crystalline silica hazard control statement must be prepared before high-risk work starts. None of these points gives permission to take the job. They tell you that a regulated route exists and that it is outside this course.

instruction.heading: Natural stone is not banned, and this course does not stretch its rules
instruction.body: WorkSafe Victoria (reviewed 27/08/2024) says the ban does not reach natural stone, and cites a granite benchtop as not prohibited. This course covers natural stone and terrazzo. The methods taught in “Pre-work surface assessment and test patches” to “Wet work on site: slurry, runoff and slip control” apply to those materials only. If a client, builder or supplier asks you to work on a surface that might be engineered stone, the answer is to stop, record the request and refer it, not to try a method that might work. Do not extend natural-stone methods to a surface that only looks similar.

procedure: Confirm the material using “Confirm the surface before work: natural stone, terrazzo or engineered stone”. If the surface is or may be engineered stone, go to step 2. If it is confirmed as natural stone or terrazzo, this lesson does not change the job.
Do not touch, abrade, cut, chemically treat or seal the surface.
Tell the client or builder, in plain words, that the work on engineered stone is regulated and that this business does not take that work.
Record the request, the surface, the identification basis and the date in the job record.
Notify the escalation contact in the business policy.
Refer the client to the WHS regulator for your state for information on the regulated route. Do not give advice that suggests the work can be done by you or the business.
Keep the record, and check the state regulator's page before you take any future engineered stone enquiry.

workedExamples.situation: A builder asks a restorer to re-polish a quartz benchtop from a 2019 kitchen so that it matches a new one. The builder says the work is simple and that the benchtop was installed legally before the ban.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: What should the restorer say and record?
workedExamples.reasoning: The surface is engineered stone, and the request is to process it. Installation before the ban does not make processing lawful. Removing or repairing installed stone is restricted, and any legacy route needs notification and controls that this business has not set up. The restorer declines the processing work in writing, records the request and the reason, notifies the escalation contact, and points the builder to the WHS regulator for the regulated route. The restorer does not suggest a method, a product or a way to do it quietly.

equipmentAndPpe: Job record form or electronic note for the enquiry and decision
Access to the business policy and the escalation contact
Current state WHS regulator web address for the job's state, checked on the day

commonErrors.error: Believing installed engineered stone must be removed by law.
commonErrors.prevention: The sources say there is no requirement to remove installed engineered stone. The restriction is on the work done to it.

commonErrors.error: Treating a ban that started in 2024 as settled and not checking the state position.
commonErrors.prevention: Check the regulator for the job's state before any engineered stone enquiry.

commonErrors.error: Doing minor modifications, such as a small chip repair, on an engineered stone top because it seems too small to matter.
commonErrors.prevention: Minor modification is named in the restricted work. Decline, record and refer.

commonErrors.error: Assuming Victorian rules apply in every state.
commonErrors.prevention: Use the regulator for the job's state.

safetyAndRegulatory.point: The national prohibition on engineered stone benchtops, panels and slabs commenced on 1 July 2024. The import ban commenced on 1 January 2025. Processing and installation are covered according to and the explanatory material; the DEWR page is silent. The WHS Regulation 529A text was not read, so that wording is partly checked. This lesson does not grant any licence, permit, exemption or authority to do engineered stone work.
Some legacy engineered stone processing may be permitted only with notification to the WHS regulator before the work starts. Completing this lesson does not satisfy any notification duty.
Stop-work rule: if a job involves engineered stone, or the material is not identified, stop, record and escalate.

qualityStandard: The material status is recorded before any engineered stone enquiry is accepted or declined.
Every declined or referred engineered stone enquiry has a written record and a referral.
Client messages do not state or imply that engineered stone work is lawful for this business.
documentationEvidence: Enquiry record: client or builder, date, requested work, and surface
Identification basis and decision (“Confirm the surface before work: natural stone, terrazzo or engineered stone” record)
Written decline or referral, with the regulator referred to
summary: Engineered stone benchtops, panels and slabs have been banned from use, supply and manufacture since 1 July 2024, with an import ban from 1 January 2025.
Installed engineered stone does not have to be removed, but work on it is restricted.
Legacy processing may need notification to the regulator before the work starts.
Natural stone is not banned, but a surface that might be engineered stone must stop until confirmed.
Decline and refer engineered stone work in writing; never suggest it can be done quietly.

knowledgeChecks.question: When did the national prohibition on engineered stone benchtops, panels and slabs commence?

1 July 2024
1 July 2025
1 January 2025

knowledgeChecks.question: When did the import ban on engineered stone benchtops, panels and slabs take effect?
options: 1 July 2024
1 July 2023
1 January 2025
1 January 2026

knowledgeChecks.question: A surface is confirmed as installed engineered stone. Which statement is correct?
options: It must be removed within twelve months of the ban taking effect on the site and the building, with the owner's sign-off
It may be ground down freely because it is already installed in the house and cannot be moved or tested
It is covered only in Victoria, not in other states or territories at all, and the rules differ greatly
There is no requirement to remove installed engineered stone, but work that removes, repairs or modifies it is restricted

knowledgeChecks.question: Which statement about notification for legacy engineered stone processing is supported by the August 2025 Safe Work Australia guidance?
options: Notification is required when work involves processing engineered stone, and the regulator does not need to approve the work before it starts
No notification is ever required for any stone processing work at all, whether the job is large or small, or whether it is inside or outside
The regulator must approve every job before it starts on the site, and the approval must be in writing from the regulator's office
Notification applies only to sealing work on finished benchtops, sinks and the surrounding edges in every house and unit across the state

knowledgeChecks.question: What does the Victorian guidance say about natural stone?
options: Natural stone is also banned in Victoria from the same date as the engineered products and the rest of the trade
The ban does not apply to natural stone, and granite is given as an example of a benchtop that is not prohibited
Natural stone needs a licence in Victoria before any work can start on the site, the house or the roof today
Natural stone is banned from 1 January 2026 in every state and territory of Australia and its islands

knowledgeChecks.question: What does the lesson say the practical point is about installed engineered stone?
options: The stone sitting in the kitchen is the problem
The colour of the benchtop
The age of the kitchen
The work is the problem, not the stone sitting in the kitchen
